about.title: About
about.intro: Most Marvel watch orders are a single flat list, release order or chronological order, which forces a rigid sequence even where the stories don’t actually depend on each other. This app takes the other approach: the catalog is a {strong}, and the “suggested order” you see is a topological sort of that graph. To watch any one title, you only need the titles that point into it.
about.source.heading: Where the graph comes from
about.source.lead: The dependency data is adapted from {link}, a community-made chart by {author} posted on r/marvelstudios:
about.source.credit: All credit for the ordering and the arrow-by-arrow judgement calls goes to its author. This project only transcribes that chart into machine-readable form so it can be walked programmatically. Quoting the chart’s own disclaimer:
about.source.disclaimer: “the labels are subjective… the lines between the levels are blurry, and the importance of a story will vary between opinions. This exists to help you navigate the MCU, but it’s not the rules.”
about.arrows.heading: The three kinds of arrow
about.arrows.lead: Each dependency carries a strength, straight from the chart’s legend. You choose how strict to be, and the order and the “what’s missing” lists both respond to that choice.
about.arrows.dashed: Dashed arrows on the original chart are predictions based on pre-release knowledge; they are flagged as {predicted} here and appear on unreleased titles.
about.artwork.heading: Posters, IMDb and streaming links
about.artwork.body1: Every title links to {imdb}, directly where we hold a verified id, and to an IMDb search otherwise, so the link always lands somewhere useful. Artwork, however, does {not} come from IMDb: it publishes no image API and its posters may not be hotlinked. Posters come from {tmdb}, whose free API permits this use and also exposes each title’s IMDb id. When no TMDB key is configured, the app draws its own poster art from the title’s data — the colour tells you which phase it belongs to.
about.artwork.body2: Streaming rights are regional and change constantly, so the platform chips are a hint rather than a promise. The {link} link on every title resolves availability for your country, and is the answer to trust.
about.summaries.heading: Detailed summaries, and spoilers
about.summaries.body1: A watch order is only useful if you are allowed to skip things. So every released title carries a {strong}: what actually happens, ending included, written so you can miss the title entirely and still follow the ones that depend on it. {count} are written so far; the rest are either not out yet or waiting for someone who has actually watched them.
about.summaries.body2: It is {never} shown unless you ask. The short, spoiler-free synopsis stays in the header where it always was; the detailed one sits below it behind a button, and its text is not in the page at all until you press it - no blur to read through and nothing for a screen reader to stumble into. If you would rather always see them, there is a checkbox next to the button, remembered in your browser under {key} and reversible from the same spot. Titles that have not come out yet have no summary, by design.
about.summaries.body3: The summaries are original prose written for this project and live in {file}. They are written in English only for now, whatever language you are reading this page in. Corrections, additions and translations are welcome - edit that one file and run {command}.
about.language.heading: Languages
about.language.body1: The interface is available in {count} languages, including right-to-left layouts for Arabic and Persian. Your browser’s preferred language is used on a first visit; after that, whatever you pick in the language menu is remembered, and the language is part of the URL so a link you share opens in the language you shared it in.
about.language.body2: What is translated is the interface. The catalog itself - title names and the detailed summaries - stays in English, because those are data rather than UI copy and a machine-translated film title helps nobody. Adding a language is one JSON file in {folder}; there is a guide in {doc}.
about.watchlist.heading: Your watchlist
about.watchlist.body: Everything you tick off is stored in your browser’s {storage} under the key {key}. There is no account, no server call and no tracking. The storage layer sits behind a small adapter interface, so a logged-in, database-backed watchlist can replace it without touching the UI. See the README for that path. You can {link} at any time.
about.data.heading: Keeping the data current
about.data.body: The whole catalog lives in one file, {file}, so adding next year’s slate means appending a title and its arrows, then running {command}. That check rejects unknown ids, duplicate or self edges, and dependency cycles before a release can ship. Exporters are included for Postgres and for Neo4j Cypher.
about.legal.heading: Legal
about.legal.body: An unofficial fan project. Marvel, the MCU and all title names are trademarks of Marvel Characters, Inc. and The Walt Disney Company; this project is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by them. It stores no media, only title names and the relationships between them.
